name: Cortistatin-14
lead: Cortistatin-14 is a naturally occurring neuropeptide related to somatostatin. It was named for its predominantly cortical expression and its ability to depress cortical activity, and it shares 11 of its 14 amino acids with somatostatin-14 even though the two peptides are encoded by separate genes.[2][7]

Its place on a looks-oriented wiki comes from two of its documented properties: it promotes slow-wave (deep) sleep in animal work, and it interacts with the growth hormone axis, binding the ghrelin-type growth hormone secretagogue receptor in human pituitary tissue.[2][6] Deep sleep and growth hormone are both topics people link to recovery, body composition and skin. Unlike somatostatin, cortistatin has been reported to bind GHS receptors, and it binds all five cloned somatostatin receptors.[2][6] More recently, structural work identified it as an endogenous agonist of the itch-related receptor MRGPRX2.[1] It is a research peptide and has no approved medical use.

No published human study has tested cortistatin-14 for any appearance-related purpose. The literature consists of basic neuroscience, receptor pharmacology and a small number of human endocrine studies.

paras: Cortistatin is expressed mainly in cortical GABAergic interneurons, and administration into the brain ventricles of rats enhanced slow-wave sleep, presumably by antagonising acetylcholine's effects on cortical excitability.[7] A review describes additional properties distinct from somatostatin, including induction of slow-wave sleep, reduced locomotor activity, and activation of cation-selective currents not responsive to somatostatin. Cortistatin mRNA follows a circadian rhythm and rises after sleep deprivation, which led the authors to suggest it is a sleep-modulatory factor.[2]
The same review asks whether a cortistatin-specific receptor exists, since the peptide acts on somatostatin receptors yet has effects somatostatin does not.[2]

Cortistatin was cloned from human, mouse and rat sources and is known to bind all five cloned somatostatin receptors, sharing many pharmacological properties with somatostatin while also having distinct physiological functions.[2][7]

A study of human pituitary membranes reported that cortistatin, but not somatostatin, bound to GHS receptors, the same receptor family targeted by ghrelin.[6] Ghrelin binding sites have also been characterised in human hypothalamus and pituitary tissue.[4]

Cryo-electron microscopy structures of MRGPRX2, a mast-cell and itch receptor, bound to cortistatin-14 were published in 2021, identifying the peptide as an endogenous ligand of that receptor.[1][5][8]

subs.h: Effects on growth hormone in humans
paras: In a study of six healthy adults, intravenous cortistatin-14 or somatostatin-14 was given and growth hormone and insulin responses measured. Cortistatin-14 inhibited basal and stimulated growth hormone secretion and insulin secretion to the same extent as somatostatin-14, and similarly reduced the growth hormone response to GHRH and to ghrelin.[9] In other words, the human data show an inhibitory effect on the growth hormone axis comparable to somatostatin rather than a stimulating one.[9]

Cloning and chromosomal mapping of mouse and human preprocortistatin were reported in 1997.[7] Reviews around 2000 characterised it as a somatostatin-family neuropeptide with its own functions,[2] and in 2001 it was reported to bind GHS receptors in human pituitary.[6] The 2021 structural work added MRGPRX2 to its known receptors.[1]

No studies of cortistatin-14 for appearance, muscle, recovery or growth outcomes were found. A human endocrine study examined the peptide's activities and its interaction with GHRH and ghrelin in six adults.[9] Other work is laboratory-based, including receptor expression in human macrophages for somatostatin receptor subtypes[3] and somatostatin knockout mouse studies.[10]
No looksmaxxing community discussion of cortistatin-14 was located.

card.summary: A somatostatin-related brain peptide that also binds ghrelin-type receptors; basic science only, nothing on looks.
card.note: No human data for any appearance use.

quick.overview:
Cortistatin-14 is a short neuropeptide closely related to somatostatin, first noted for its activity in the cortex. It has been studied in receptor pharmacology and neuroscience.

No published trial has tested it for appearance, muscle or recovery, and it is not an approved drug.
quick.mechanism: It binds all five somatostatin receptors, has been reported to bind GHS (ghrelin-type) receptors in human pituitary, and activates the itch receptor MRGPRX2.
quick.risks: Human safety data are essentially limited to small endocrine studies. It has no approved product or regulatory status as a medicine.

chain: Brain peptide induces slow-wave sleep in animal studies

angle.text: Cortistatin-14 is discussed because of its overlap with sleep regulation and the growth hormone axis, both of which people connect with recovery and physique. This is a mechanistic connection from laboratory and endocrine studies; no trial has measured appearance outcomes.
